video_title: Stellar Hits $4B+ in RWA's: Why Wall Street Institutions Are Choosing Stellar | Denelle Dixon
transcript: So they actually sent the asset cross border. They sent it from the United States to one of their treasury side in Europe. They then were able to demonstrate they first they minted it, then they sent it and used it as payment and redemption. And then they were able to say, okay, I want to claw back the asset and then I want to freeze the asset. They went through the whole life cycle to make sure that it all worked. This is important. >> [music] >> All right, Denelle, it's so great to have you back >> on The Defiant. >> Thank you so much. It's wonderful to see you and great to be here. >> So Denelle Dixon is the CEO and executive director of the Stellar Development Foundation. And you know, we we already covered the basis of Stellar at The Defiant. So today I want to talk specifically about RWAs and tokenization because it's been kind of the theme and and trend for crypto in the past few months. And specifically for Stellar, you've seen a lot of growth there. So you just got to roughly 4 billion in tokenized real world assets. That's 360% annual growth. So what's driving this growth? >> Yeah, I love the number. I love the trend line. It's like such a great way for us to demonstrate all the hard work we've been doing. I mean, the truth of the matter is it started way way back when at the inception of the network when we were really focused on asset issuance and payments. So asset issuance is like a cornerstone of what we do. We the network actually does a really good job of doing it. Keeps it really simple. But so much of the number that you're we're talking about in terms of crossing the 4 billion mark has to do with the work we did last year. Like bringing those partners that came to us that really wanted to tokenize assets and that already had the plan and they they wanted to be able to see the growth and the distribution happen. And we're seeing the fruits of that labor this year. And we've continued so that number is going to continue to grow and it's a really really important trend line to be able to watch just because it demonstrates the institutional side that's coming to the net a network like Stellar because of what the network is really good at. And it makes me really happy to see the number. The trend line is important and tells a lot of the story. The activity of what's going on with these assets is also important in terms of being able to be used as collateral on lending and borrowing. So there's a lot of really good stuff that's happening on the network. So the number is important, but everything else that surrounds it is also important. >> Totally. And I'll definitely get to those points. Um but specifically which issuers are the main ones uh driving this 4 billion figure? >> Well, uh fun that we had and we celebrated 5 years of growth with Franklin Templeton who they were the first entity to issue a money market fund and they did so on Stellar. They started the process in 2019, which is crazy, but they actually issued their asset in 2021, I believe. And so we just crossed the 5-year mark with them and there's a lot of growth with Benji, their asset. Interestingly, a lot of growth on Stellar in a lot of different holders on Stellar, which I love to see because it's not just like three institutions that hold it. It's a lot of retail side and institutional side that hold that asset. We also see Speiko that has been doing just a really nice job of getting their asset distributed. And it demonstrates that, you know, and and again, every entity sort of approaches it from what makes sense to them. Like is this an institutional asset? Is it a retail asset? Is it specific? Is it for a sweep fund? Are there there's different things that we have to look at with those assets, but um a lot of different players, but we're seeing, you know, we're seeing private credit, we're seeing money market funds, we're seeing a lot of different types of assets on chain, which is exactly the kind of variety that you want. >> But still Speiko is about 1.55 billion of of tokenized assets. So how do you think about concentration? >> Oh, so I actually don't really think about concentration in a bad way. I think about it is that's exactly what we want to see. Not in terms of concentration. We don't want to see just like one issuer have all of the the the assets that are on the network. But when you see that they've got to product market fit and they see those assets being utilized and uh being purchased by their either their institutional side or the retail side, I love to see that because it demonstrates that the network is working for them and that's what we want to see. That's not the case with respect to the 4 billion though. You see lots of players be contributing to that and lots of different asset types contribute to it. So, I'm not worried about concentration at all. I think that that just demonstrates again product market fit, the true focus on distribution, which always tends to be a little bit of an issue in uh on the when you're using blockchain. When these entities come, they think they're going to get new users and sometimes they do. But net new users from their other assets and so sometimes they're seeing that growth and sometimes maybe the growth isn't hitting everything that they want because some of they might be cannibalizing some of their old users. But that's expected cuz it's an asset that everybody not people don't care whether people aren't going to it just because it's a digital asset. They're going to it because it's a money market fund that that drives yield. >> Yeah. >> So, I think it's an interesting discussion to have, but I think that uh we're going to continue to see growth in these numbers. As I said, continue to see a lot of different players come to the network. We have already some in the queue. So, I'm not worried about the um the the numbers, but I love to see product market fit. It makes me so happy because that's exactly what we wanted from the beginning. >> Totally. And I think that um that approach of saying people shouldn't buy these assets because just because they're digital assets, but you know, because they serve some some purpose. And so that takes me to my next question, which is um we've we've as an industry made a lot of progress uh like I said, past few few months in bringing in in tokenizing tokenizing assets on chain. Um but there's been less progress in putting those assets to work. So, yeah, there's you know, T-bills on on chain, private credit on chain, but very I I've seen the stats, it's like less than 10% that are actually being used actively in DeFi. So, how do you think about that question in Stellar? >> Yeah, it's a really important question. We need to put these real-world assets to use. We call it RWA-Fi because you want to be able to blend the DeFi world with the RWAs. So, you need to have the certain controls that allow the asset issuers to be able to, you know, freeze and do the clawbacks and do all those things that they feel comfortable with even in the DeFi space. Part of what they get when they issue an asset on Stellar. But, the one thing that you need, which actually was just highlighted by one of the folks in our industry, Redstone, who can can provide this and sort of fill this gap is that when you're dealing with RWAs, you don't always have the 24-hour price analysis, right? And so, that's a little bit of the missing link. Redstone is a player that's actually providing that on Stellar. And so, they saw this need and now they can provide that sort of price analysis 24 hours and that brings it so that then you can use RWAs in RWA-Fi, for example, and be able to use those assets in DeFi. That's a really, really important piece. One of the things I love is that as we grow as an industry I I I always talk about like the the idea that you see cracks sometimes and you need to be able to fill those cracks in. And when the ecosystem jumps in to fill it, it shows that you're actually all holistically doing your job. So, I love that Redstone saw this need, is building for it, and that hopefully we'll be able to see more RWAs get brought into that space so you can put those to work not just as collateral but lending, borrowing, lots of different opportunities. >> Right, but but you're right. I think Yeah, first step was tokenizing assets and then next steps is filling those those gaps or those cracks. Like, yeah, like 24/7 pricing, may maybe figuring out kind of the the regulatory issues, compliance, like all those things that kind of make them usable as collateral in DeFi and and things. >> Well, that's an important piece, too, because I mean, you think about compliance, this is exactly what these issuers needed at the outset. They needed to know that they could actually make it composable for them. And that's what you can do on Stellar, is that you can choose when you want to be able to have whether you want to be able to have all those tools, clawback freezing, I think most asset issuers do, but then when you KYC, do you KYC, is it authorization required, so it's an asset you have to KYC before. All of those things are there now. Again, like [clears throat] those were base layer pieces that were built into the protocol, just getting everybody comfortable with them. But then seeing these gaps and figuring out who can fill the gaps in, make it so that the ecosystem continues to grow and expand, and that's really what you want to see. >> So, let's talk about uh um two big announcements you had last week. Um US Bank uh issuing its stablecoin with Stellar, um MoneyGram working with Rain and Stellar for uh their stablecoin credit card. Uh tell me about these announcements. >> Yeah, we've had so so much great uh news out there in the world over the last 6 months, and this is this last couple of weeks has been like a driver of some of this really uh great content. US Bank uh announced that it had a pilot on with Stellar back in November of last year. And what they announced last week was that they actually did the transactions to to use the pilot to show that all the steps that they needed to work, the full life cycle of what any asset asset issuer wants to see, they did. So, they actually uh sent the asset cross-border, they sent it from the United States to um one of their treasury side in Europe. They then were able to demonstrate they first they minted it, then they sent it and used it as payment um and redemption. And then they were able to say, "Okay, I want to clawback the asset, and then I want to freeze the asset." They went through the whole life cycle to make sure that it all worked. This is important. It's important because US Bank is one of the top five institutions in the United States. To have a top five be able to focus on making sure that this works for them and to see the success demonstrates ample opportunity for what's next. There's a lot of right now banking consortiums that are out there thinking about issuing stablecoins and then you look at US Bank and they've already done this, right? They've issued the asset, now they've actually tested it in their pilot and the next steps they have they'll be the ones to decide what's next, but it makes me really happy to see that kind of progress even without clarity um and the clarity act you have the genius act that allows them to do this kind of thing. So, it's great from the US to see that. So, that's the US Bank side and it's kind of also remarkable. I mean, may not be like crypto time, but if you think they announced their pilot in November and they they used their pilot in within 9 months is a pretty great thing. Yeah. Um for for an old institution like that. And then on the MoneyGram piece, this has just been years of work with MoneyGram. This is a 75-year-old institution who's really embraced the ability to bring its infrastructure to uh crypto into the blockchain world to be able to allow wallets to use the infrastructure to get payments and to get redemptions of uh uh for that last mile in different regions and in 200 location 200 uh countries around the world. Really important. This next step for them was now they're going to use their uh their wallet and then they're starting in Colombia and allow them to use the stablecoin asset and use it as a debit. And so, they can use debit cards and that and to be able to make these payments everywhere. That's a pretty uh bold step for them and I see it growing outside of in growing using their digital wallet and just growing um outside of Colombia and that is also like great progress. 75-year-old institution doing these kinds of things really taking and using this technology for what it's valuable for. >> Um these two announcements are are so interesting because I think they're they're just great examples of um you know, some of the the the biggest uh They're they're they're examples of of just like great product market fit that uh blockchains have shown in well in the real world, right? It's like a US bank nothing to do with with US bank nothing to do with crypto it's not a crypto bank it's not like it's not even like a like a tech related bank that you would think it's not a Silicon Valley bank but they are you know piloting how to use stable coins in in this like very real way making sure it works for them and then MoneyGram like a really old financial institution and when you know from the very beginning everyone kind of knew that blockchain should be used for remittances because you know cross-border payments is where you can get efficiencies but just now in kind of these past few months these past years when we see it actually coming to like they're actually starting to use these rails so it's it's really exciting to see. >> Well, I think that is absolutely true and it just like it is the reason why I'm here and the reason why I spend so much time focusing on making these rails simple and easy to use because it is the people that didn't necessarily have access to money market funds to any yield bearing assets to being able to get remittances at the right cost that now do using this tech stack. The one thing I'll say too that's really cool about these two announcements and these aren't the only two that sort of demonstrate it but I kind of love it. We kind of talk about it as like a barbell and you have on the one side the retail side for MoneyGram so they're actually reaching those people in all parts of the world right now they're focused on Colombia with this this this debit card but they are reaching like the retail users they're reaching the individuals in Colombia that now have access to be able to use these digital assets and simplify their life using this card and then on the US bank side it's an institution that is focused on its own treasury at this point that's what they did the the the pilot that's what they used the pilot to do but the institutional side and the retail side, all in one network doing both sides of it, and I love that. >> So, why do you think they picked Stellar specifically? >> I think that it's because Stellar has been was built for purpose. Stellar was built for this purpose. We were talking about stablecoins way back when when stablecoins were not a thing. We always wanted value to move not with volatile crypto assets. We wanted it to move with stable assets that were backed by instruments. We used to call them US dollar backed instruments, but then it was also peso backed instruments. We had When I first started, so almost 8 years ago, we actually had about, I'd say, 40 different stablecoins. We didn't call them stablecoins, but these assets that were backed throughout the world. They were It was too early. It was like one of those things where they came in, everybody was really excited about moving value. The network was built for this. You have all those controls, those compliance controls at that level that you can use. And so, we had started way back then with these institutions doing that. Now, the truth is, not very many of those are still around because they were built in the early days, but it's just because they didn't achieve product market fit until many years later. So, now we actually see that this is like the de facto standard, but it's something that we wanted from the very beginning, and we saw it, and that's the path that we went down. So, I think that those controls are really important from a compliance standpoint. Privacy is also really important. Institutional privacy becomes like this piece that every institution asks about. And the same thing that we did with the compliance side, we've done with privacy. It's composable. You get to choose what you need to use, whether you want to be in like a privacy pool, whether you want to have the token itself be private, or whether the transactions are blurred in terms of like who's receiving them. These are all things institutions get to choose. So, we listen to the market. We also kind of helped to set the standard in the market by doing that by making this tech work in the way that works for them. So, it's That's why I think that they choose Stellar and will continue to choose Stellar because they can feel comfortable the tech is going to grow with them. >> So, another huge institution that also chose Stellar as one of the few blockchain partners was the DTCC. Um they announced Stellar as a partner in May. Uh they've been kind of getting ready to roll out the the um um mainnet or or the operational side in I think it it's in November. Can you fill me in on where that's at? >> So, in terms of their dates, I don't know if their date where their dates are right now, but they did I believe they went to testnet in July with parts of it um and they still have work to do that they're working to get um the actual underlying tech on their side up and running. With respect to what they're doing with Stellar is we have always focused on they've indicated to us that it's going to be the first half of 2027 and we are still on track for that. We work with them every day. We have a great team on our side and a great team on their side from a technical standpoint that have uh different metrics and milestones they need to hit uh and they're doing that. I'm just so excited about them first of all choosing Stellar because it made a whole lot of sense just in terms of an open public network is what an institution like that should build on. We believe very uh firmly in that and I think that a lot of other people out there in the world do see open networks as being the ones that are going to be able to compete and change and grow um and make it so that liquidity and everything is really simple uh instead of being in a closed environment. Um and I also see trillions of dollars coming on to on to on chain and that and some of that money is going to come on to Stellar. Hopefully a lot of it given that there's not very many blockchains they're going to be put into their system. So, it makes me really happy to see them first of all tokenizing the assets and recognizing that for every company you're going to need to like move with the pace of technology and they've done that. That's a really old institution, too. So, when you think about some of the oldest institutions moving to this tech stack, it just makes a lot of sense. And I think it's going to bring a lot of value to their asset issuers, and ultimately to the consumers of those. >> So, um we we we talked about this a little bit, but if you can expand on the the assurances that institutions need to see to to take the these steps. I mean, they they are already doing it, tokenizing assets, um but what what kinds of requirements are you hearing, and how is Stellar fulfilling them? >> Yeah, I really I think that some of the most important ones are the ones that are just making sure the tech is stable. And Stellar has a 99.99% uptime just in the last 10 years. And it's been around for 14 years. And even during that, we had one small blip where there was an outage for like 42 minutes or something like that in 2019, actually 2 weeks after I started. But other than that, we have 99.99% uptime. That's crazy. That's important. That's really valuable to them. They care about that. You cannot have a network outage impact a DTCC in the in the ability to for them to deliver to their customers. So, that's one thing that's really important. Those compliance controls and allowing them to decide what they need, cuz again, some assets might be off-required assets, so that you want that authorization before they hold it. Some could be free-floating assets, and that no one needs to have that, but you still want that clawback and that freeze. Well, it's really easy to do that on Stellar. And then I do think that the privacy piece is a really important piece of it. I think we're going to hear more and more about this. We've built I think Stellar has the most native implementation of the the the building blocks for privacy than any other chain, any other public open chain, and I think that's really important because it allows those issuers to determine what they need, whether how as I said, how they can implement privacy themselves. And so, those are it's it's not just those things, but it's the fact that we are moving before they are and allowing those pieces to be part of what they can actually take advantage of is really important. So, we're not waiting for them to tell us, "Oh, we need this." It's already built in. It's already part of it. We started building for institutions from day one. And it's actually one of the funny things is that sometimes I was always like, "Guys, we don't have a billion users out here using this asset yet. So, we can like we need to we can think about how we're going to implement this in our tech stack. We can't always let the perfect be the enemy of the good." But we're going to have that soon. And so, we need to think about like what that looks like. And so, we are definitely approach every release. We we do more releases now a year because we approach every release as making the updates that's necessary for the network, but also like future proofing the network each time. So, it's really it's pretty cool to see the evolution of it and where it started and where it's at now. >> And by the way, for those listening, um definitely check out the privacy documentary that the fine print did together with Stellar, um which well, in my biased opinion, I think was a pretty good way of of showing the capabilities. Um I'd love to if you can just like highlight the importance of Stellar being an open permissionless network and and and, you know, why why that's significant uh for the bringing institutions on chain because yeah, maybe there's some misconception or a myth that um institutions can only use permission networks. Why I mean, how how do you counter that argument? >> Oh, I don't even think it's a question anymore. I think that open public networks are what institutions are using and they're very comfortable with it. Uh I think in the early days there was that question about whether they should or whether they, you know, should build their own or they should use a network that's like permissions so they can control it. I think part of the reason why we got ourselves into the the the I'm going to call it a mess, the mess that we're in with respect to the software that institutions have been using for the last 75 years is that it hasn't been updated because it's not open. Closed source software gets updates for sure. I'm not There's nothing against closed source software, but when you're dealing with a financial institution that wants to reach users all over the world and wants to reach its its clients and its partners all over the world, integration and making sure that everyone has access to the same software is really important. The way to do that is to use an open public network. We're very comfortable doing so many things on online now. Just think about the days when maybe we couldn't have the video calls that we have or we couldn't actually send the information that we could. Well, the internet lets us do that. The internet is the best example of an open public network that works for everyone. So, that actually teaches us that using using an open public network that is a financially focused network for this kind of financial services piece makes all the sense in the world. It complete It gets improved all the time by people all over the world. You are constantly checking for bugs. Not only do we have bug bounty programs, we also do bug checks with every AI version that comes out. We do bug checks on the network itself, but lots of people care about the value of the network and they do the same thing. So, that we're constantly improving the network that way. We have people that are running the network that are and and doing the governance of the network that are institutions that have issued assets. That's important cuz they care about the future state of the network. So, you have a lot of players that care about it. And just in terms of the connectivity, the liquidity, the ability to reach people all over the world, that's what an open public global network allows. So, I don't think that there's a choice now. I think everyone recognizes that this is where we can go, especially one that has all the tools that Stellar has to be able to use to to effectuate whatever need you have from an institutional side. >> And speaking of participation, it's been interesting to see how institutions are slowly shifting from being issuers to being actual validators of a blockchain networks. Can you talk about this and how it's happening on Stellar? >> Yeah, it's funny cuz institutions first started doing this on other networks because it was staking and they were getting staking rewards and that was what institutions, which is kind of always ironic to me, uh that institutions were comfortable playing in that space. But what we see, and I think more importantly to see it on a chain like Stellar, you don't you we don't have validator incentives. The only incentive for validators to participate in the governance of the network, which is the the to become a validator, is because they care about the future of the network. So they're incentivized to do that because they want to be able to ensure that they're going to have all these features that we currently have, that we're going to improve and grow them. And so cuz validators get to decide whether to accept any um updates to the chain. And so for us, it's exactly what we wanted. We wanted this from day one. We wanted all asset issuers to be able to have issuer enforced finality, to be able to make sure that they're part of the uh governance of the network. And so it's all like coming to the exact place that we want to be able to see. Uh so we see a lot more institutions focused there. We bring validators on in threes um from a from a tier one validator set. Validators can join if they choose to, but to the tier one network is the one that actually does a lot of the uh the the governance piece. And so the the tier one network brings people on being brings validators on in threes. And so we've seen a lot of growth there and it makes me really happy to see that. >> Nice. And then to to wrap up, um you've been in this space for for a long time and it's always kind of a cycle of booms and busts. Uh and every time it's like it feels like we're on the verge of something of, you know, like at at a pivotal moment of adoption of mainstream um adoption coming, institutions are coming. Like we've been hearing this forever. Um this time it feels different, but uh is it because we're kind of in this in the inside or is it actually different? >> I think uh I think it's a little bit of both. I think that these bus these these retractions and these expansions are really important to the growth of anything. If I look back on my early days in web two and web in the late part of web one is that you saw the web grow immensely during the boom. And everybody was doing everything and nobody had a business model, nobody had a plan. It was just like throw like the fact that you're on the internet and you can just [music] like in I in the early days of crypto and you're going to get you're going to raise and you're going to be able to go out and put your business out there. The retraction is then what kept the people in the market that were serious, that actually had business plans, that actually were were providing value to their end users, whoever they might be, institutional side or retail side. And I think we're seeing some of that now in these markets. And so I think that expansion is just like the boom period that you need to be able to test the tech to make sure the tech is actually heading in the right direction, that every that it has all the tools that it needs to have in it. And then the retraction period is when builders build. We're in a retraction we're in a retraction in terms of like the crypto market and the bear market, but other than that like it is booming with respect to what's happening with this tech stack. And so I feel like there no longer can be a question that this tech stack is valuable because we have so many institutions building on it. So there's those questions of like will this be around? Yes, it's going to be around. Those are all settled, but there's going to be something new that we're all going to have to figure out like how do we do this? Like purpose is something that's coming to a couple of chains. We I really would love to see some of that on Stellar as well. These are things that are pushing in in terms of financial services, they're pushing the envelope a little bit in terms of what's out there. We're going to see equities come and hopefully be natively issued. There's a couple companies that have done that already, but native issuance on chain there's just so much more to see. So I feel like it's a little bit that we're inside the bubble and we're like, "Yay, we're finally here." But also, there's like a lot of redemption outside to say, "This tech stack actually works for what it was intended to." And we're going to see more payments, too, I think. And then once you see cross-border payments, then it's actually going to be a full circle moment like, "Yes, this is exactly what we wanted to happen." >> Awesome. Well, I think that's a great place to wrap then. As always, a pleasure having you. >> Thank you so much. A great to be here.
